question: How do you structure folders in a large React codebase?
shortAnswer: Organise by feature rather than by file type, so everything a feature needs lives in one folder and deleting the feature deletes one directory. Keep genuinely shared code in a separate shared or common area, and enforce the boundaries with lint rules so features do not start importing each other's internals.
memoryHook: Group by feature, not by file type. If deleting a feature means visiting eight folders, the structure is wrong.
answer:
## Type-based vs feature-based

```text
❌ By type — a feature is scattered across every folder
src/
  components/   Button, UserCard, InvoiceRow, ChartTooltip…  (200 files)
  hooks/        useUser, useInvoice, useChart…
  utils/        formatDate, calculateTax, parseCsv…
  types/

✅ By feature — a feature is one folder
src/
  features/
    invoices/
      components/  InvoiceRow.tsx  InvoiceTable.tsx
      hooks/       useInvoices.ts
      api/         invoiceApi.ts
      types.ts
      index.ts     ← the public surface
    auth/
    dashboard/
  shared/
    components/    Button, Input, Modal
    hooks/         useDebounced, useMediaQuery
    lib/           fetcher, formatting
  app/             routes, layouts, providers
```

The test: **how many folders do you visit to delete a feature?** One, or eight.

---

## The barrel file as a public API

```ts
// features/invoices/index.ts — the only sanctioned entry point
export { InvoiceTable } from './components/InvoiceTable';
export { useInvoices } from './hooks/useInvoices';
export type { Invoice } from './types';
```

Everything else in the folder is private by convention. That lets you refactor internals without breaking consumers.

> Caveat worth mentioning: large barrel files can hurt tree-shaking and slow down bundlers. Keep them small and per-feature, not one root barrel re-exporting everything.

---

## Enforce the boundaries

Conventions decay unless they are checked:

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "import/no-restricted-paths": ["error", {
      "zones": [{
        "target": "./src/features/*/!(index.ts)",
        "from": "./src/features",
        "message": "Import from the feature's index.ts, not its internals"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

Also worth encoding: `shared/` must never import from `features/`. Dependencies point inward.

---

## Where things go

| Code | Location |
|------|----------|
| Used by one feature | Inside that feature |
| Used by two features | Leave it duplicated for now |
| Used by three or more | Promote to `shared/` |
| Routing and providers | `app/` |

Promoting too early is the more common mistake. Two similar-looking implementations that later diverge are cheaper than one shared abstraction with five boolean flags.

---

## Colocation

Tests, stories and styles live next to the file they describe — `InvoiceRow.tsx`, `InvoiceRow.test.tsx`, `InvoiceRow.stories.tsx`. A parallel `__tests__` tree means every rename touches two places and tests quietly rot.

---

## The honest note

Any consistent structure beats an inconsistent good one. The cost of a mediocre convention is small; the cost of five conventions in one repository is large. Decide, document it in the README, and enforce it in CI.

question: What is a monorepo and when is it the right choice?
shortAnswer: A monorepo holds multiple packages or apps in one repository with shared tooling, so a change spanning several packages is one atomic commit and one pull request. It is right when teams share code heavily and coordinate releases; it is wrong when teams are genuinely independent, because you pay real tooling and CI cost for coordination you do not need.
memoryHook: Monorepo buys atomic cross-package changes and pays for it in build tooling. Worth it when code is shared, not when teams are separate.
answer:
## What it looks like

```text
repo/
  apps/
    web/            Next.js app
    admin/          Vite SPA
    mobile/         React Native
  packages/
    ui/             design system
    config/         eslint, tsconfig, tailwind presets
    api-client/     generated types + fetchers
    utils/
  turbo.json
  package.json      workspaces
```

---

## The real benefit

```text
Multi-repo:  change ui → publish v2.1 → open PR in web → open PR in admin
             → three reviews, version skew while they land

Monorepo:    one PR changes ui, web and admin together
             → CI proves nothing broke → merged atomically
```

Atomic cross-package change is the thing you are buying. Everything else is secondary.

---

## The costs, honestly

| Cost | Detail |
|------|--------|
| CI time | Naively, every push builds everything |
| Tooling | Turborepo or Nx becomes load-bearing |
| Git operations | Slow on very large repos |
| Ownership | Needs `CODEOWNERS` or everyone reviews everything |
| Release coordination | Independent versioning requires Changesets |

The CI problem is solved by **task caching and affected-only builds**:

```json
// turbo.json
{
  "tasks": {
    "build": { "dependsOn": ["^build"], "outputs": ["dist/**", ".next/**"] },
    "test": { "dependsOn": ["^build"] },
    "lint": {}
  }
}
```

```bash
turbo run build --filter=...[origin/main]   # only what the diff affects
```

With remote caching, a package nobody touched is restored from cache in seconds rather than rebuilt. Without that, a monorepo becomes painful quickly.

---

## When to choose it

| Choose monorepo | Choose multi-repo |
|-----------------|-------------------|
| Shared design system across apps | Genuinely independent products |
| Types shared between frontend and backend | Different release cadences and owners |
| Frequent cross-cutting refactors | Different languages and toolchains |
| One team, several surfaces | Open-source packages with outside contributors |

---

## Versioning

**Fixed** — everything shares a version. Simple; forces unnecessary releases.
**Independent** — each package versions on its own. Use Changesets:

```bash
npx changeset          # describe the change and its semver bump
npx changeset version  # bumps versions, writes changelogs
```

---

## The nuance to raise

> "A monorepo is not a monolith. Packages can still deploy independently — you are colocating source, not coupling runtime. Conversely, a multi-repo setup can still be tightly coupled. The repository layout and the architecture are separate decisions."

question: What are micro-frontends and what are the trade-offs?
shortAnswer: Micro-frontends split an application into independently built and deployed pieces owned by separate teams, composed at runtime through Module Federation or at build time. They solve an organisational problem, not a technical one, and the costs are real: duplicated dependencies, harder shared state, inconsistent UX and much more complex debugging.
memoryHook: Micro-frontends solve a team-coordination problem. If you have one team, they are pure cost.
answer:
## The problem they address

One repository, one deploy pipeline, forty engineers across six teams. Every release requires coordinating everyone, one team's bug blocks another's launch, and the release train runs weekly because that is the only way to synchronise.

Micro-frontends let each team build, test and deploy their slice independently.

> The framing that matters: **this is Conway's law applied deliberately.** The architecture exists to match the org chart. If your org chart does not look like that, you do not need it.

---

## Composition approaches

| Approach | How | Trade-off |
|----------|-----|-----------|
| **Route-based** | Reverse proxy routes `/checkout` to a separate app | Simplest; full page load between apps |
| **Build-time** | Each team publishes an npm package | Easy; loses independent deploy |
| **Module Federation** | Runtime import of remote modules | True independence; most complex |
| **Web components** | Each app exports a custom element | Framework-agnostic; awkward interop |
| **Server-side composition** | Edge assembles fragments | Fast, good SEO; needs infrastructure |

---

## Module Federation

```js
// Host
new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  remotes: { checkout: 'checkout@https://checkout.example.com/remoteEntry.js' },
  shared: {
    react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^19.0.0' },
    'react-dom': { singleton: true },
  },
});
```

```jsx
const Checkout = lazy(() => import('checkout/CheckoutApp'));
```

`singleton: true` on React is essential — two React copies means hooks break with confusing errors. It also means every micro-frontend must agree on a React major version, which quietly removes some of the independence you were buying.

---

## The costs

| Cost | Reality |
|------|---------|
| **Bundle size** | Shared deps help, but duplication is common |
| **Shared state** | Auth and cart across boundaries needs a custom event bus or shared store |
| **Consistent UX** | Needs a versioned design system everyone actually upgrades |
| **Debugging** | A stack trace crosses three independently deployed apps |
| **Integration testing** | Nobody's CI runs the whole thing |
| **Version skew** | A stale remote deployed against a changed contract |
| **Performance** | Extra network requests, more JS overall |

---

## Cheaper alternatives to try first

1. **Monorepo with clear package boundaries** — most of the ownership benefit, far less complexity
2. **Feature flags** — teams merge continuously and release independently behind flags
3. **Route-level code splitting** — team-owned bundles without runtime federation
4. **Trunk-based development with strong CI** — often the actual fix for slow releases

---

## How to answer

> "I would want to see the coordination pain first. Below roughly 30–50 engineers, a well-structured monorepo with feature flags usually gets you independent deploys at a fraction of the cost. Micro-frontends are the right answer when teams genuinely cannot ship without waiting for each other — and I would still expect a shared design system and a shared auth contract."

Enthusiasm for micro-frontends without naming the costs reads as inexperience.

question: How do you migrate a large codebase incrementally, for example class components to hooks?
shortAnswer: Never do a big-bang rewrite. Stop the bleeding with a lint rule preventing new class components, migrate opportunistically when you are already touching a file, and use codemods for mechanical changes. Track progress with a metric so it stays visible, and accept that some files may never migrate.
memoryHook: Stop the bleeding first, then migrate what you touch. A rewrite branch that runs for six months never lands.
answer:
## Why big-bang rewrites fail

A six-month migration branch conflicts constantly with the main branch, delivers no value until it lands, and gets abandoned when priorities shift. Meanwhile new code is still being written in the old style.

---

## The strategy

**1. Stop the bleeding.** Make the old pattern impossible for new code:

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "react/prefer-stateless-function": "error",
    "no-restricted-syntax": ["error", {
      "selector": "ClassDeclaration[superClass.name='Component']",
      "message": "New components must be function components with hooks."
    }]
  }
}
```

This alone changes the trajectory — the problem stops growing even before you fix any of it.

**2. Migrate what you touch.** "Boy Scout rule": if you are already changing a file for a feature or a bug, convert it. The work rides along with tests you were writing anyway.

**3. Codemod the mechanical parts.**

```bash
npx jscodeshift -t transform.js src/ --parser=tsx
```

Codemods handle the repetitive 80% — import updates, API renames, prop signature changes. They cannot handle judgement calls, so review every diff.

**4. Prioritise the rest by value.** Components that are heavily edited, cause the most bugs, or block a feature. Not alphabetically.

---

## Make progress visible

```bash
# Track it, chart it, put it in the team channel
echo "Class components: $(grep -rl 'extends React.Component' src/ | wc -l)"
```

An invisible migration loses to whatever is visible. A number that goes down each sprint keeps it alive.

---

## Both patterns must coexist

This is what makes incremental migration possible at all:

```jsx
// A class component can render a function component and vice versa.
// Context, refs and props all work across the boundary.
class LegacyPage extends React.Component {
  render() { return <ModernWidget data={this.state.data} />; }
}
```

The same is true of most React migrations — Pages Router beside App Router, Redux beside React Query, CSS Modules beside Tailwind. Verify the interop story before committing to a path.

---

## Other migrations, same shape

| Migration | Bridge |
|-----------|--------|
| Pages → App Router | They coexist in one Next.js app |
| Redux → React Query | Move server state first; leave client state |
| JavaScript → TypeScript | `allowJs`, then file-by-file, `strict` last |
| Webpack → Vite | Run both; switch dev first, build later |
| CRA → Vite | One-time, but do it in a spike with a rollback |

---

## Knowing when to stop

Some files are stable, rarely touched and work fine. Migrating them is cost with no return. "90% migrated, the remaining 10% is dead-stable legacy we will convert if we ever touch it" is a legitimate and mature end state — say so rather than pretending 100% is always the goal.

question: How do you set up error monitoring and observability for a React app?
shortAnswer: Capture errors with an error boundary reporting the component stack, plus global handlers for unhandled promise rejections, and send them to a tool like Sentry with source maps uploaded so traces are readable. Add release tagging so you know which deploy broke, and track real user Web Vitals rather than only lab scores.
memoryHook: Error boundary plus unhandledrejection plus source maps plus release tag. Without source maps the stack is minified noise.

question: How do you manage bundle size in a growing application?
shortAnswer: Measure with a bundle analyser first, then attack the biggest items: split by route, lazy-load heavy libraries, replace oversized dependencies, and ensure tree-shaking actually works. Add a size budget to CI so regressions are caught in the pull request rather than discovered months later.
memoryHook: Analyse, then budget in CI. Bundle size only ever grows unless something blocks it.
answer:
## Measure first

```bash
npx vite-bundle-visualizer          # Vite
ANALYZE=true npm run build          # next/bundle-analyzer
npx source-map-explorer dist/*.js   # any build
```

The treemap almost always contains a surprise — a date library, an icon set, or a locale bundle nobody knew shipped.

---

## The usual offenders

| Culprit | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| `moment` (~70KB + locales) | `date-fns` with named imports, or `Intl` |
| `lodash` whole import | `import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'` or `es-toolkit` |
| Icon libraries | Import individual icons, not the barrel |
| Chart libraries | `lazy()` — only on pages that render charts |
| Locale data | Load the active locale only |
| Polyfills | Target modern browsers; check your browserslist |

```js
// ❌ Pulls the entire library in many setups
import _ from 'lodash';
import * as Icons from 'react-icons/fa';

// ✅
import debounce from 'lodash/debounce';
import { FaUser } from 'react-icons/fa';
```

---

## Split by route first

```jsx
const Admin = lazy(() => import('./features/admin/AdminApp'));
```

Highest value for the least effort — most users never visit most routes. Then split heavy components that are conditionally rendered:

```jsx
// The editor bundle only downloads when someone actually edits
const RichTextEditor = lazy(() => import('./RichTextEditor'));
```

---

## Tree-shaking requirements

It only works when:

1. The package ships **ESM** (`"module"` or `"exports"` in package.json)
2. The package declares `"sideEffects": false`
3. You import named exports, not a namespace
4. The bundler runs in production mode

A CommonJS-only dependency cannot be tree-shaken at all. Checking `"sideEffects"` when evaluating a library is a good habit to mention.

---

## Budget it in CI

```yaml
- uses: preactjs/compressed-size-action@v2
  with:
    pattern: 'dist/**/*.{js,css}'
```

Or `size-limit` with a hard threshold:

```json
{ "size-limit": [{ "path": "dist/index.js", "limit": "180 KB" }] }
```

Without a gate, bundle size only goes up — each PR adds a little and nobody notices until the app is slow. A comment on the PR showing "+34KB" changes behaviour immediately.

---

## Keep perspective

Before optimising 20KB of JavaScript, check whether the page ships a 2MB unoptimised hero image or three third-party analytics scripts. Those are usually larger and easier to fix.

And measure **compressed** size — Brotli or gzip is what actually crosses the network, and it changes the ranking of what matters.

---

## The bigger lever

Server Components remove component code from the bundle entirely rather than merely deferring it. For content-heavy applications that is a larger structural win than any amount of splitting.

question: How do you design a CI/CD pipeline for a frontend application?
shortAnswer: Run fast checks first — typecheck, lint, unit tests — then build once and reuse that artefact for every later stage so you deploy exactly what you tested. Add preview deployments per pull request, and gate merges on the checks rather than on someone remembering to run them.
memoryHook: Build once, deploy that artefact everywhere. Rebuilding per environment means you ship something you never tested.
answer:
## Pipeline shape

```yaml
jobs:
  verify:
    steps:
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run typecheck     # fastest, fails most often
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test -- --coverage

  build:
    needs: verify
    steps:
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4   # ← build ONCE
        with: { name: dist, path: dist/ }

  e2e:
    needs: build
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4  # ← test THAT artefact
      - run: npx playwright test

  deploy:
    needs: [build, e2e]
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4  # ← deploy THAT artefact
      - run: ./deploy.sh
```

**Build once, promote the artefact.** Rebuilding per environment means production runs a binary that no test ever saw — dependency resolution, timestamps and env substitution can all differ.

---

## Order matters

Cheapest and most likely to fail goes first. Typecheck in 20 seconds catches more than E2E in 12 minutes, and failing fast keeps the feedback loop tight.

---

## Environment variables at build vs runtime

This catches people out with static frontends:

```text
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL is baked into the bundle at BUILD time.
So "build once, deploy to staging and prod" breaks if they need different URLs.
```

Options:

1. Use a **relative** `/api` path and let the environment route it — cleanest
2. Fetch runtime config from `/config.json` on boot
3. Build per environment, accepting the duplication

Option 1 removes the problem entirely and is worth naming.

---

## Preview deployments

Every pull request gets its own URL. This is the single highest-value addition — designers and product reviewers stop needing a local setup, and "works on my machine" conversations disappear. Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages do it automatically.

---

## Speed

| Technique | Effect |
|-----------|--------|
| Cache `node_modules` by lockfile hash | Saves 1–3 min per job |
| `npm ci`, not `npm install` | Faster and deterministic |
| Run independent jobs in parallel | Wall-clock time drops |
| Turborepo remote cache | Skip unchanged packages entirely |
| Shard E2E across runners | 12 min becomes 3 |
| Only run E2E on the merge queue | Trade some feedback for speed |

---

## Deployment strategy

Static frontends deploy atomically — upload the new assets, then flip the index. Keep the **previous build's chunks available** for a grace period, or users with an open tab get a chunk-load error on their next lazy navigation.

Rollback should be re-pointing to the previous build, not a revert-and-rebuild. Measure it: if rolling back takes 20 minutes, incidents last 20 minutes.

---

## Gates worth having

Required status checks, at least one review, a bundle-size comment, and a preview URL. Anything advisory gets ignored under deadline pressure.

question: How do you handle API contracts between frontend and backend teams?
shortAnswer: Generate types from a schema rather than hand-writing them — OpenAPI or GraphQL codegen means the compiler catches a breaking change instead of your users. Validate responses at runtime with something like Zod, because a generated type is a promise the server can break, and version the API so old clients keep working during a rollout.
memoryHook: Generate types from the schema, validate at the boundary anyway. A TypeScript type is a hope, not a check.
answer:
## The problem

```ts
// Hand-written and now a lie — the backend renamed it to fullName last sprint
interface User { id: string; name: string; }
```

TypeScript believes you. Nothing fails until a user sees `undefined`.

---

## Generate, do not hand-write

```bash
# From an OpenAPI spec
npx openapi-typescript ./openapi.yaml -o ./src/api/schema.d.ts

# GraphQL
npx graphql-codegen
```

Wire it into CI so a backend change that breaks the contract fails the frontend build immediately — the whole point is moving the discovery from production to the pipeline.

---

## Types are not runtime checks

```ts
// ❌ An assertion, not a verification
const user = await res.json() as User;

// ✅ Validate at the boundary
const UserSchema = z.object({ id: z.string(), fullName: z.string() });
const user = UserSchema.parse(await res.json());   // throws with a clear message
```

Validate where data enters the system — API responses, `localStorage`, URL params, `postMessage`. Inside your own code, trust the types.

The payoff: instead of `Cannot read property 'toUpperCase' of undefined` five components deep, you get *"Expected string at user.fullName, received undefined"* at the fetch call.

---

## Process, not just tooling

| Practice | Effect |
|----------|--------|
| Schema is reviewed before implementation | Disagreements surface in a PR, not in QA |
| Additive changes only within a version | Adding a field never breaks a client |
| Deprecate before removing | Mark it, wait, then delete |
| Version breaking changes | `/v2/users`, both live during migration |
| Contract tests in both CI pipelines | Backend cannot merge a break unnoticed |

The key rule: **removing or renaming a field is breaking; adding one is not.** Design changes as additions wherever possible.

---

## Unblocking parallel work

Agree the schema first, then mock it so the frontend does not wait:

```js
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

export const handlers = [
  http.get('/api/users/:id', ({ params }) =>
    HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id, fullName: 'Ada Lovelace' })
  ),
];
```

MSW intercepts at the network layer, so the same handlers serve local development and tests, and swapping to the real API needs no code change.

---

## BFF, when it is justified

If the frontend needs five calls to render one screen, a backend-for-frontend that aggregates them is worth considering. It removes waterfalls and lets the client own its own contract shape. The cost is another service to run and deploy — worth it for a complex product, overkill for a small one.

GraphQL solves the same problem differently, at the cost of caching complexity and query-depth concerns.

question: How do you decide whether to build or buy a piece of functionality?
shortAnswer: Buy or adopt when the problem is solved, well-maintained and not your differentiator — auth, payments, date pickers, rich text. Build when it is core to your product, when the library is a poor fit you would fight constantly, or when the maintenance burden of a dependency exceeds writing it. Judge the total cost, not the initial one.
memoryHook: Buy the undifferentiated, build the differentiator. And the cost of a library is the upgrade path, not the install.
answer:
## The default

Use a library for anything that is not your product's differentiator, especially where correctness is hard and the failure modes are subtle:

| Do not build | Why |
|--------------|-----|
| Authentication | Security-critical; a mistake is a breach |
| Payments | PCI compliance; a mistake is a fine |
| Date pickers | Timezones, locales, keyboard, accessibility |
| Rich text editors | `contenteditable` is genuinely brutal |
| Combobox / select | The ARIA pattern has dozens of edge cases |
| Data fetching cache | Race conditions, deduplication, invalidation |
| Virtualisation | Variable heights are hard |
| Charting | Scales, axes, accessibility |

These all have years of edge cases baked into mature libraries. Reimplementing them means rediscovering the same bugs.

---

## When to build

**1. It is your differentiator.** Figma did not use an off-the-shelf canvas. If the thing is why customers pay you, own it.

**2. The library fits badly.** Fighting an abstraction for six months costs more than writing the 400 lines you actually need. The signal: you are reading library source to work out how to defeat it.

**3. The dependency cost is disproportionate.** A 40KB library for one function you could write in fifteen lines.

**4. The library is unmaintained.** Last publish two years ago, open security advisories, no response to issues. Adopting it means adopting it.

---

## Evaluating a dependency

| Check | Signal |
|-------|--------|
| Weekly downloads | Adoption, and how quickly bugs get found |
| Last publish | Under 6 months is healthy |
| Open issues vs closed | Is anyone answering? |
| Bundle size | bundlephobia — and does it tree-shake? |
| Dependency count | Each one is transitive risk |
| TypeScript support | First-class, or `@types` maintained by strangers? |
| Licence | MIT/Apache fine; AGPL needs legal review |
| Escape hatch | Can you replace it in a week if it fails? |

That last one matters most. A library behind your own thin wrapper can be swapped; one whose API is spread across 300 files cannot.

---

## The cost people underestimate

> The cost of a dependency is not installing it. It is upgrading it for the next four years, debugging it when it breaks in a way the docs do not cover, and migrating off it when it is abandoned.

Equally, the cost of building is not writing it. It is owning it forever — the edge cases, the accessibility, the browser quirks, and the person who wrote it leaving.

---

## How to answer

Name a real decision you made and what you traded. "We used React Hook Form rather than building form state because validation and field arrays are where hand-rolled forms rot — but we wrote our own toast system because the libraries we tried all fought our design system, and toasts are 150 lines." That reads as judgement, not preference.

question: How do you keep code quality high across a large team?
shortAnswer: Automate everything that can be automated — formatting, linting, types, tests in CI — so review time is spent on design rather than style. Then invest in the things automation cannot do: clear conventions written down, a shared component library, and code review focused on correctness and clarity rather than preference.
memoryHook: Automate taste out of code review. Humans should argue about design, never about semicolons.
answer:
## Automate the mechanical

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "format": "prettier --write .",
    "lint": "eslint . --max-warnings 0",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"
  },
  "lint-staged": {
    "*.{ts,tsx}": ["eslint --fix", "prettier --write"]
  }
}
```

Prettier ends every formatting argument permanently — nobody has an opinion because nobody has a choice. That reclaims a surprising share of review time.

`--max-warnings 0` matters: warnings nobody must fix accumulate until they are all ignored, including the important ones.

---

## The rules that actually catch bugs

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "react-hooks/rules-of-hooks": "error",
    "react-hooks/exhaustive-deps": "warn",
    "@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises": "error",
    "jsx-a11y/click-events-have-key-events": "error"
  }
}
```

Those four prevent conditional hooks, stale closures, unhandled promise rejections, and inaccessible click handlers — four of the most common real defects in React code.

---

## Code review that is worth the time

| Review for | Not for |
|------------|---------|
| Is it correct? Edge cases? | Formatting — Prettier decides |
| Is it the right abstraction? | Naming preferences with no rationale |
| Will the next person understand it? | "I would have done it differently" |
| Security and performance implications | Rewriting to your personal style |
| Are the tests meaningful? | Coverage percentage as a goal |

Conventions worth adopting: reviews within one working day, small PRs (under ~400 lines gets a real review; 2,000 gets "LGTM"), and distinguishing blocking comments from suggestions explicitly — prefix non-blocking ones with `nit:`.

---

## Write the conventions down

An undocumented convention is a hazing ritual. A short `CONTRIBUTING.md` covering folder structure, naming, state management choices, testing expectations and the PR process saves the same conversation forty times.

Use ADRs for significant decisions — a one-page record of what was chosen, what was rejected and why. Six months later nobody remembers, and the ADR prevents relitigating it.

---

## Shared foundations

A design system means the accessible, tested `<Button>` is easier to use than writing one. Making the right thing the easy thing does more for consistency than any amount of review.

---

## What does not work

| Approach | Why it fails |
|----------|--------------|
| Coverage thresholds | Produces tests that assert nothing |
| Style guides without automation | Nobody reads them |
| A single gatekeeper reviewer | Bottleneck, and a bus factor of one |
| Big-bang refactor sprints | Never scheduled; never finished |
| Advisory-only CI checks | Ignored under deadline |

---

## The framing

> "Quality comes from making the correct path the path of least resistance. If doing it properly requires discipline, it will not survive a deadline. If it is automated or already built, it survives everything."

question: How do you handle deploys without breaking users who have the app open?
shortAnswer: Keep the previous build's chunks available after a deploy, because a user with an open tab will request filenames that no longer exist and get a chunk load error on their next lazy navigation. Catch that error with a boundary offering a reload, and poll a version endpoint to prompt users onto the new build gracefully.
memoryHook: The open tab still has the old JS. Keep old chunks alive, catch chunk-load errors, offer a reload.

question: How do you approach performance budgets and Core Web Vitals?
shortAnswer: Set explicit thresholds for LCP, INP and CLS plus a bundle size cap, enforce them in CI so regressions block the pull request, and monitor real user data because lab numbers on a fast laptop mislead. Track the seventy-fifth percentile, not the average, since averages hide the users having a bad time.
memoryHook: LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1 — at p75, from real users, not your laptop.
answer:
## The three metrics

| Metric | Measures | Good | Common cause when bad |
|--------|----------|------|----------------------|
| **LCP** | When the main content appears | < 2.5s | Unoptimised hero image, slow TTFB, render-blocking JS |
| **INP** | Responsiveness to interaction | < 200ms | Long tasks, heavy re-renders, third-party scripts |
| **CLS** | Visual stability | < 0.1 | Images without dimensions, injected banners, font swap |

INP replaced FID in 2024 and is much harder to pass — it measures every interaction through to the next paint, not just the first input delay. Heavy React re-renders show up here directly.

---

## p75, not average

```text
Average LCP: 2.1s   ✅ looks fine
p75 LCP:     4.8s   ❌ a quarter of users are having a bad time
```

Google grades on p75 for exactly this reason. Averages are dominated by fast devices on fast networks — the people who were never the problem.

---

## Enforce it in CI

```yaml
- uses: treosh/lighthouse-ci-action@v11
  with:
    urls: https://preview-url.example.com
    budgetPath: ./budget.json
```

```json
[{
  "resourceSizes": [
    { "resourceType": "script", "budget": 180 },
    { "resourceType": "image", "budget": 400 },
    { "resourceType": "total", "budget": 800 }
  ],
  "timings": [
    { "metric": "largest-contentful-paint", "budget": 2500 }
  ]
}]
```

A budget that does not block a merge is a wish. Make it a required check, with a documented process for raising it deliberately when a feature justifies it.

---

## Lab vs field

| | Lighthouse (lab) | RUM (field) |
|---|------------------|-------------|
| Environment | Simulated, consistent | Real devices and networks |
| Use for | Catching regressions in CI | Knowing the actual experience |
| Weakness | Not your users | Noisy, needs volume |

You need both. Lab catches the regression in the PR; field tells you whether it matters. Chrome UX Report data is what Google actually uses for ranking.

---

## The React-specific levers

| Metric | React fix |
|--------|-----------|
| **LCP** | Server-render or statically generate; preload the hero image; never lazy-load it |
| **INP** | Break up long tasks; `useTransition` for expensive updates; virtualise long lists; defer third-party scripts |
| **CLS** | Explicit image dimensions; reserve space for async content; `font-display: optional` or preload fonts; never inject banners above existing content |

Third-party scripts deserve special mention — analytics, chat widgets and tag managers are frequently the single largest INP contributor, and they are usually somebody else's decision.

---

## Making it stick

Attach it to something the business cares about. "LCP is 3.8s" moves nobody; "every 100ms of latency costs roughly 1% of conversion, and we are 1.3s over budget" gets prioritised. Performance work that is not framed in product terms loses to feature work every time.

question: How do you document a frontend codebase so it stays useful?
shortAnswer: Prefer documentation that lives next to the code and breaks when it is wrong — types, Storybook stories, and tests read as examples. Reserve prose for the things code cannot express: why a decision was made, how to run things, and architectural constraints. Documentation that duplicates the code will rot.
memoryHook: Document the why, not the what. The code already says what it does — and it is never out of date.
answer:
## The hierarchy

| Form | Rots? | Best for |
|------|-------|----------|
| **Types** | Never — the compiler checks them | Shapes, contracts |
| **Tests** | Never — CI checks them | Behaviour and edge cases |
| **Storybook** | Rarely — it renders real components | Component usage and states |
| **ADRs** | No — they are historical by design | Why a decision was made |
| **README** | Slowly | Setup, commands, structure |
| **Wiki prose** | **Fast** | Almost nothing |

Prefer forms that break when they become wrong. A comment claiming a function returns a string will happily lie forever; a type will not.

---

## Comments explain why

```ts
// ❌ Restates the code
// Loop through users and filter active ones
const active = users.filter((u) => u.isActive);

// ✅ Explains something the code cannot
// The API returns soft-deleted users with isActive=false rather than omitting
// them, because the reporting service needs the historical rows. See PLAT-441.
const active = users.filter((u) => u.isActive);
```

The test: **would a competent developer be surprised, or waste time rediscovering this?** If yes, comment it. If the code already says it, do not.

---

## Architecture Decision Records

```markdown
# ADR-012: Use React Query for server state

## Status
Accepted — 2026-03-14

## Context
Server data was in Redux. We were hand-writing caching, deduplication and
refetch logic, and had three separate race-condition bugs in one quarter.

## Decision
React Query owns all server state. Redux keeps only client state
(currently: cart draft and editor preferences).

## Consequences
+ Removed ~1,400 lines of thunk and reducer code
+ Deduplication and revalidation come free
− Two state systems to learn
− Redux DevTools no longer shows server data

## Rejected alternatives
SWR — smaller, but weaker mutation and pagination support for our use case.
```

One page, written once, never updated — superseded by a new ADR instead. This is the highest-value documentation a team can keep, because six months later nobody remembers the reasoning and the decision gets relitigated.

---

## The README that matters

Someone joining on Monday needs: how to run it, how to run the tests, where things live, how to deploy, and who to ask. Five sections. Anything longer stops being read.

The strongest signal of a healthy README is that a new joiner can get the app running without asking anyone — make that an explicit test by having the next new starter try, and fix whatever blocked them.

---

## Storybook as living documentation

```jsx
export const Loading = { args: { status: 'loading' } };
export const WithError = { args: { status: 'error', error: new Error('Failed') } };
export const Empty = { args: { items: [] } };
```

States rendered as stories are simultaneously documentation, a visual regression baseline and a development harness. They cannot drift because they render the real component.

---

## What not to write

A wiki page listing every component and its props — the types already do that, and the page is wrong within a month. Documentation that duplicates something machine-checkable is a liability, not an asset.

question: How do you manage technical debt on a product team?
shortAnswer: Make it visible and quantified — tie each item to the cost it imposes in bugs or slowed delivery — then pay it down continuously rather than requesting a dedicated refactor sprint that never gets scheduled. Distinguish deliberate debt taken for a reason from accidental debt, and be willing to leave stable debt alone.
memoryHook: Quantify the interest, pay it inside feature work. A refactor sprint you have to ask permission for never happens.
answer:
## Frame it as cost, not aesthetics

```text
❌ "The checkout code is messy and I don't like it."

✅ "Checkout has caused 40% of our production incidents this quarter.
    Any change there takes about three days instead of one because there
    are no tests and the state is spread across six components.
    Two weeks of work would remove most of that."
```

The second gets funded because it is an argument about delivery speed and reliability. The first sounds like preference.

---

## The four quadrants

| | Deliberate | Accidental |
|---|-----------|------------|
| **Prudent** | "Ship it now, refactor after launch" | "Now we know how it should have been built" |
| **Reckless** | "No time for tests" | "What are tests?" |

Prudent-deliberate debt is a legitimate engineering tool — it buys time. The requirement is that it is **recorded** and has a trigger for repayment, otherwise it silently becomes permanent.

---

## Paying it down

**Continuously, inside feature work.** When you touch a file, improve it. Budget roughly 20% of each sprint. This survives deadline pressure because it is not a separate negotiable line item — a dedicated "refactor sprint" gets cut the first time a deadline slips.

**Strangler pattern for large items.** Build the replacement beside the old code, route traffic gradually, delete the old path once nothing uses it. No long-lived branch.

**Automate the ratchet.** New code must meet the standard even if old code does not:

```json
{ "rules": { "no-restricted-imports": ["error", { "paths": ["legacy-store"] }] } }
```

The problem stops growing immediately, which changes the trajectory even before anything is fixed.

---

## Make it visible

Track debt items in the same backlog as features, with an estimated cost. Chart a metric that moves — remaining class components, files without tests, `any` count, p95 build time. An invisible problem loses to a visible one every time.

---

## Debt worth leaving

> Code that is ugly, stable, rarely touched and working is not costing you anything. Refactoring it is pure risk with no return.

Only repay debt that is charging interest: code you change often, code that breaks often, code that blocks new work. Being able to say "we chose not to fix that, and here is why" is a stronger answer than claiming everything must be clean.

---

## The conversation with product

Do not ask for permission to do engineering work — build it into the estimate. "This feature is two weeks" can legitimately include the refactor that makes it two weeks instead of three.

When debt genuinely needs its own project, bring numbers: incident counts, cycle time, on-call load. Product managers respond to "we ship 30% slower in this area", not to "the code is bad".

question: How do you support older browsers without penalising modern ones?
shortAnswer: Define a browserslist based on real analytics rather than guessing, let the build target it so you are not shipping unnecessary transpilation and polyfills, and use progressive enhancement so a missing feature degrades rather than breaks. Modern and legacy bundles served conditionally give old browsers support without taxing everyone else.
memoryHook: Set browserslist from analytics, not fear. Every unnecessary polyfill taxes the 98% to serve the 2%.

question: How do you onboard a new developer onto a large frontend codebase?
shortAnswer: Get them running and shipping something small in the first day or two, because reading code without changing it teaches very little. Pair them with a buddy, give them a real but contained first ticket, and treat every question they have to ask as a documentation bug to fix.
memoryHook: Ship on day one. Every question a new joiner asks is a gap in the docs — fix it while they are asking.
answer:
## Week one

| Day | Goal |
|-----|------|
| 1 | App running locally; one trivial PR merged (a typo, a copy change) |
| 2 | Codebase tour with their buddy; understand the folder structure |
| 3–5 | A real but contained ticket — a small bug in a well-tested area |

The day-one merge matters more than it sounds. It proves the environment works end to end, exercises the whole PR and deploy pipeline, and gives a sense of progress in a week that otherwise feels like drowning.

---

## Setup must be one command

```bash
git clone … && cd app && npm install && npm run dev
```

If it takes a day and three people to get running, that is a defect affecting every future hire. Time it with each new joiner and fix whatever blocked them — that same blocker will hit the next five people.

A devcontainer or Docker setup removes the "works on my machine" class of problem entirely.

---

## The buddy system

One named person whose job is to answer questions. Without it, new joiners spend an hour deciding whether a question is worth interrupting someone for — and usually decide it is not, then stay stuck.

Say explicitly: **"Ask after 15 minutes of being stuck."** New people systematically over-estimate how long they should struggle.

---

## The first ticket, chosen well

| Good | Bad |
|------|-----|
| Small, contained scope | Cross-cutting refactor |
| In a tested area | The untested legacy module |
| Real user value | Made-up busywork |
| Touches the full pipeline | Frontend-only trivia |

A real ticket beats a toy task — it teaches the workflow, the review culture and the deploy process at the same time.

---

## Treat questions as documentation bugs

> Every question a new joiner asks is a gap in the docs, and they are the only people who can see it.

Ask them to open a PR against the README with the answer they were given. Onboarding docs written by people who already know things always assume too much; docs improved by the person who just struggled are accurate.

---

## What to explain that code cannot

- **Why** things are the way they are — the ADRs
- Which areas are stable and which are known-fragile
- Who owns what, and who to ask about which domain
- The deployment and on-call process
- Team norms: review turnaround, when to ask, what "done" means

This context is what actually takes months to absorb. Writing it down compresses that.

---

## Set expectations honestly

Six months to full productivity in a large codebase is normal. Saying so up front removes a lot of quiet anxiety — otherwise capable people conclude they are underperforming because they cannot navigate 300,000 lines in three weeks.

---

## How to answer this in an interview

If asked as "how would you onboard someone", it is really asking whether you think about the team beyond your own output. Concrete practices — buddy, first-day PR, docs-as-you-go — read far better than "I'd give them a tour of the codebase."
